definition: Contiguous means sharing a common border or touching along an edge, with no gap in between.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word contiguous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know contiguous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Their two farms were contiguous, separated by nothing more than a low stone wall that both families had mended for generations.
Two distant islands are separated by miles of open water — nowhere near the direct, edge-to-edge contact that contiguous demands.
Two picnic blankets spread a few feet apart on the lawn are nearby, but only when their edges actually touch, with no grass showing between them, do they become contiguous.

Adjacent means next to or very near, but it does not strictly require touching — two adjacent lots can sit side by side with a narrow gap between them. Contiguous is stricter: contiguous things actually touch, sharing a border with no gap at all.

Adjoining spaces are physically connected, usually through one shared wall or partition, like adjoining offices. Contiguous is the broader, more technical term for touching along any common edge — two contiguous counties share a border without sharing anything like a wall.

Abutting is the technical word, common in law and architecture, for meeting exactly edge-to-edge at a boundary line, as when a driveway abuts the street. Contiguous covers the same no-gap contact but describes the whole relationship of bordering, not just the line where the edges meet.
Standing physically apart, separated by a gap or open space — a detached house sits on its own, sharing no wall with its neighbors.
Having no point of contact or link at all — where contiguous things meet along a shared edge, disconnected things have a clean break between them.

Contiguous means sharing a common border or touching along an edge, with no gap in between.
The hotel gave us two contiguous rooms joined by a connecting door, so the kids could reach our room without ever stepping into the hallway.
Contiguous describes things that share a common boundary and touch with no gap in between.
These two rooms are not merely close, or on the same floor — they meet along a shared wall, and the connecting door proves they are directly joined.
Compare this with rooms that are only 'nearby': those might sit several doors apart, with other rooms wedged between them.
The defining test for contiguous is direct contact — if you can fit anything at all between the two things, even a hallway or one empty room, they are close but not contiguous.
Contiguous is a precise, somewhat formal word common in geography, law, real estate, and even computing (as in 'contiguous memory').
Reach for it when you specifically mean 'touching with no gap'; in casual speech, 'next to' or 'side by side' usually sounds more natural.

The wildlife trust had bought forest for years, but by 2015 its maps showed a problem: twenty parcels scattered like torn paper across the valley.
Elk do not commute between separated woodlots.
For a corridor to work, the protected land had to be contiguous, each parcel sharing a true border with the next.
Two tracts divided by a single farm road might as well be miles apart, because animals funneled onto pavement rarely cross.
So the trust changed strategy.
It stopped chasing the cheapest acres and began paying premiums for the thin strips that stitched neighbors into one unbroken run.
The final purchase, a nine-acre seam between the two largest blocks, closed the last gap.
A hiker can now walk the whole preserve without leaving it once.
